x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Judge me, O Jehovah, for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in Jehovah without wavering.
x.Darby: [A Psalm] of David. Judge me, O Jehovah, for I have walked in mine integrity, and I have confided in Jehovah: I shall not slip.
x.KJV: A Psalm of David. Judge me, O Lord; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the Lord; therefore I shall not slide.
x.YLT: By David. Judge me, O Jehovah, for I in mine integrity have walked, And in Jehovah I have trusted, I slide not.

nt: By **Vindicate me**, David means that he wants God to prove to others that he is innocent of wrongdoing. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Prove that I am righteous] or [Show others that I am innocent]

Here David is using an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please vindicate me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **integrity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for I have done what is right] or [for I have lived uprightly]

Here David is speaking of his manner of living and conducting himself as if it were a path he **walked**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for I have lived with integrity] or [for I have acted with integrity]

x.ASV: Examine me, O Jehovah, and prove me; Try my heart and my mind.
x.Darby: Prove me, Jehovah, and test me; try my reins and my heart:
x.KJV: Examine me, O Lord, and prove me; try my reins and my heart.
x.YLT: Try me, O Jehovah, and prove me, Purified are my reins and my heart.

nt: David is using imperatives to make polite requests rather than to give commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests in your language, you could use a form that communicates a polite request. Alternate translation: [Please examine me, Yahweh, and test me; please try]

These two phrases, **Examine me** and **test me**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, examine and test me]
See how you translated the similar phrase “The righteous God examines hearts and kidneys” in [7:9](../007/009.md). Alternate translation: [try my motives and my thoughts]

x.ASV: For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes; And I have walked in thy truth.
x.Darby: For thy loving-kindness is before mine eyes, and I have walked in thy truth.
x.KJV: For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes: and I have walked in thy truth.
x.YLT: For Thy kindness is before mine eyes, And I have walked habitually in Thy truth.

nt: David is using **before my eyes** as a common expression of his culture to mean “constantly in my thoughts” or “always in my awareness.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am always mindful of your covenant faithfulness] or [I constantly remember your covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For the way you are faithful to your covenant]

David is speaking of living according to God’s truth as if it were a path he could **walk about** on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I live according to your truth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in what is true]

x.ASV: I have not sat with men of falsehood; Neither will I go in with dissemblers.
x.Darby: I have not sat with vain persons, neither have I gone in with dissemblers;
x.KJV: I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers.
x.YLT: I have not sat with vain men, And with dissemblers I enter not.

nt: Here, **sit** represents associating with or spending time with people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not associate with men of falsehood]

The phrase **men of falsehood** refers to people who are characterized by dishonesty, deception, or lies. David is describing those who habitually speak or act falsely. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceitful people] or [dishonest men]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [lying men] or [men who lie]

The implication is that these people are concealing their evil intentions or dishonest behavior. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will not go with those who hide their evil deeds] or [and I will not go with those who hide their evil deeds and intentions]

x.ASV: I hate the assembly of evil-doers, And will not sit with the wicked.
x.Darby: I have hated the congregation of evil-doers, and I have not sat with the wicked.
x.KJV: I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked.
x.YLT: I have hated the assembly of evil doers, And with the wicked I sit not.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones who do evil things] or [the ones who act wickedly]
See how you translated the similar phrase “I do not sit with” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [and I will not associate with]
See how you translated the phrase “the wicked” in [1:1](../001/001.md).

x.ASV: I will wash my hands in innocency: So will I compass thine altar, O Jehovah;
x.Darby: I will wash my hands in innocency, and will encompass thine altar, O Jehovah,
x.KJV: I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O Lord:
x.YLT: I wash in innocency my hands, And I compass Thine altar, O Jehovah.

nt: Washing hands **in innocence** was a symbolic action by which David showed that he had not done anything wrong. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I demonstrate my innocence by washing my hands]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **innocence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as an innocent person] or [because I am innocent]

x.ASV: That I may make the voice of thanksgiving to be heard, And tell of all thy wondrous works.
x.Darby: That I may cause the voice of thanksgiving to be heard, and declare all thy marvellous works.
x.KJV: That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works.
x.YLT: To sound with a voice of confession, And to recount all Thy wonders.

nt: The expression **to cause to be heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to proclaim] or [to make known]

x.ASV: Jehovah, I love the habitation of thy house, And the place where thy glory dwelleth.
x.Darby: Jehovah, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwelleth.
x.KJV: Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.
x.YLT: Jehovah, I have loved the habitation of Thy house, And the place of the tabernacle of Thine honour.

nt: David is speaking of the tabernacle of Yahweh as if it were a **house**, which Yahweh makes his **habitation** or dwelling place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your tabernacle] or [the tabernacle where you are present in a special way]

David is using this possessive form, **habitation of your house**, to mean the place where Yahweh has made his special **habitation** (dwelling place). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the house where you dwell]

x.ASV: Gather not my soul with sinners, Nor my life with men of blood;
x.Darby: Gather not my soul with sinners, nor my life with men of blood;
x.KJV: Gather not my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloody men:
x.YLT: Do not gather with sinners my soul, And with men of blood my life,

nt: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not gather]
אַל־תֶּאֱסֹ֣ף עִם־חַטָּאִ֣ים נַפְשִׁ֑⁠י וְ⁠עִם־אַנְשֵׁ֖י דָמִ֣ים חַיָּֽ⁠י

David assumes that readers will know that **gather** refers to God gathering wicked people to judge them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Do not cause me to die and be judged along with the sinful, nor let me perish in judgment with men of blood] or [Do not take me away to be judged along with the sinful, nor let me perish in judgment with men of blood]
Here David is using the term **my soul** to mean himself, his very life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [me]

David is using the adjective **sinful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [sinful people]

David is using the possessive form to describe **men** that are characterized by violence and bloodshed. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent men] or [murderers]

x.ASV: In whose hands is wickedness, And their right hand is full of bribes.
x.Darby: In whose hands are evil devices, and their right hand is full of bribes.
x.KJV: In whose hands is mischief, and their right hand is full of bribes.
x.YLT: In whose hand is a wicked device, And their right hand is full of bribes.

nt: Here, **hands** represents what these evil men do (their actions) or plan to do. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who plan an evil scheme]

The phrase **their right hand is full of bribes** could mean: (1) that these wicked men are in positions of authority and they accept bribes and make unjust decisions or rulings as a result. Alternate translation: [and their right hand is full of bribes which they have accepted] or (2) that these evil men give bribes to those in positions of authority in order to influence them to make wrong and unjust decisions. Alternate translation: [and they give bribes] or [and they pervert justice by giving bribes]

x.ASV: But as for me, I will walk in mine integrity: Redeem me, and be merciful unto me.
x.Darby: But as for me, I will walk in mine integrity. Redeem me, and be gracious unto me.
x.KJV: But as for me, I will walk in mine integrity: redeem me, and be merciful unto me.
x.YLT: And I, in mine integrity I walk, Redeem me, and favour me.

nt: See how you translated the similar phrase “for I have walked in my integrity” in verse 1.

In this context, David is using imperative forms to make polite requests to God rather than to give commands. The words **redeem me and be gracious to me** are requests for God’s help and mercy. If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests in your language, use a form that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please redeem me and be gracious to me]

x.ASV: My foot standeth in an even place: In the congregations will I bless Jehovah.
x.Darby: My foot standeth in an even place; in the congregations will I bless Jehovah.
x.KJV: My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the Lord.
x.YLT: My foot hath stood in uprightness, In assemblies I bless Jehovah!

nt: Here David is speaking as if his **foot stands on level ground**. He means that he is in a stable and secure position because he has lived righteously. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am secure because I have lived righteously]

David assumes that readers will know that **assemblies** refers to gatherings of God’s people for worship. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the gatherings of God’s people I will bless Yahweh]
